name: Semaglutide
lead: Semaglutide is a peptide medication that mimics the gut hormone glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and acts as a GLP-1 receptor agonist. Developed by Novo Nordisk, it is sold as Ozempic and Rybelsus for type 2 diabetes and as Wegovy for chronic weight management, and is given as a weekly injection or, in the case of the oral products, a daily tablet [1][16]. It was approved in the United States in 2017 and in Canada, the European Union and Japan in 2018 [1].

In clinical trials of adults with overweight or obesity and no diabetes, semaglutide at the 2.4 mg weekly dose produced average weight reductions in the range of roughly 12 percent of body weight over 68 weeks or longer, compared with small losses on placebo [4][5][14]. Large outcome trials have also reported lower rates of major cardiovascular events in people with diabetes and in people with obesity and established cardiovascular disease [15][11].

In looksmaxxing communities, semaglutide is discussed as a systemic fat-loss tool whose effects on the face follow overall fat loss; the drug has no known mechanism for targeting facial fat specifically. The phrase "Ozempic face" describes the gaunt or hollowed facial appearance that some people report after large, rapid weight loss on GLP-1 drugs [17]. Documented adverse effects are mainly gastrointestinal, and the US label carries a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodents [16]. Unregulated or compounded semaglutide products are also discussed online.

paras: Semaglutide is indicated in the United States to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes and to reduce major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk [16][1]. Under the brand name Wegovy it is indicated for long-term weight reduction in people aged twelve and over with obesity, and in adults with overweight and at least one weight-related condition, and to reduce cardiovascular events in adults with established cardiovascular disease who are overweight or obese [1]. Wikipedia also lists use in metabolic-associated steatohepatitis under Wegovy and Kayshild [1].
Semaglutide is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines, and in 2024 it was among the most commonly prescribed medicines in the United States [1].

Appearance-focused users take semaglutide to lose body fat through reduced appetite. The weight loss is systemic rather than targeted, so any change to the face results from overall fat reduction [2][17]. Some people use prescription products; others, according to forum posts, use compounded or research-labelled supply obtained outside conventional prescribing [26][22]. Trials of the drug enrolled people with overweight or obesity (typically a BMI of 27 or 30 and above) or with type 2 diabetes, and no published trial has tested it in lean people seeking cosmetic leanness [14][4].

In the STEP program, once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg was tested as an adjunct to lifestyle intervention. STEP 1 enrolled 1,961 adults with obesity or overweight and no diabetes [14]. A 2022 meta-analysis of four randomized trials (3,613 people without diabetes) found a mean weight reduction of 11.85 percent favoring semaglutide over control [4], and a 2024 meta-analysis of four trials of at least 68 weeks (3,087 people) reported a weighted mean difference of about -12.1 percent relative to placebo [5]. In people with type 2 diabetes, STEP 2 compared 2.4 mg with 1.0 mg and placebo and examined weight outcomes in that group [9]. The two-year STEP 5 trial reported effects over a longer period [13].

Comparative trials place semaglutide below tirzepatide for weight loss. In a 2025 open-label phase 3b trial in adults with obesity without diabetes, the maximum tolerated dose of tirzepatide was compared directly with the maximum tolerated dose of semaglutide [3]. In the STEP 8 trial semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly was compared with daily liraglutide 3.0 mg [12].

Body composition has been studied in meta-analyses. A 2025 network meta-analysis of 22 randomized trials (2,258 participants) found that GLP-1 receptor agonists reduced total body weight, fat mass and lean mass, with lean-mass loss accounting for roughly a quarter of total weight loss; relative lean mass, as a percentage of body mass, was not significantly changed [6]. Wikipedia summarizes a 2024 review in which lean mass fell by 0 to 40 percent in individual studies while the ratio of lean to total mass rose [1].

Maintenance has also been examined. In STEP 4, participants who continued semaglutide after a run-in period were compared with those switched to placebo [10]. A 2025 meta-analysis of eight randomized trials in people with a BMI of at least 27 examined weight after GLP-1 drugs were stopped [7], and Wikipedia, citing a 2025 systematic review, states that people regain on average about two-thirds of lost weight within a year of stopping [1].

The most common adverse effects are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain and constipation. They are dose-dependent, usually mild to moderate, and tend to peak during dose escalation before easing [1]. A meta-analysis of semaglutide trials in people without diabetes found gastrointestinal adverse events were about 1.6 times as likely as on control [4]. Delayed gastric emptying can cause indigestion and, rarely, gastroparesis or bowel obstruction; gallstone and other biliary disease is also associated with treatment [1].

The US label carries a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors, based on rodent studies, and the drug is contraindicated in people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 [16]. The label also lists acute pancreatitis, diabetic retinopathy complications, hypoglycemia when combined with insulin or insulin secretagogues, acute kidney injury from volume depletion, and severe gastrointestinal reactions [16]. Wikipedia notes that cardiovascular outcome trials have not shown a statistically significant increase in pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer and that early retinopathy worsening has been attributed to rapid glucose lowering [1]. A meta-analysis of 21 trials of GLP-1 receptor agonists (99,599 patients) assessed mortality, cardiovascular events and serious adverse events [8].

The label says data in pregnancy are insufficient to evaluate risk and that animal studies suggest potential fetal risk [16]. Wikipedia reports that in January 2026 the FDA asked for removal of suicidal behavior and ideation warnings from GLP-1 receptor agonist labels [1].

The "Ozempic face" label has been used for facial hollowing, volume loss and skin laxity after fast, substantial weight loss. A 2024 dermatology article addresses whether the phenomenon reflects weight loss itself or the drug [17]. Men on semaglutide forums discuss facial fat loss as an expected consequence of leaning out [22].

Semaglutide is a GLP-1 analogue with about 94 percent sequence homology to the human hormone. It binds and activates GLP-1 receptors, reducing appetite and increasing satiety through brain pathways, slowing gastric emptying, and enhancing glucose-dependent insulin secretion while suppressing glucagon [16][1]. Weight loss is attributed mainly to reduced energy intake [1].

Compared with human GLP-1, semaglutide lacks the first six amino acids and has substitutions at two positions, including 2-aminoisobutyric acid, which blocks breakdown by dipeptidyl peptidase-4. A fatty-diacid chain attached to a lysine promotes albumin binding, which extends the half-life to about seven days and supports weekly injection [1][16].

Semaglutide is prescription-only in the United States and elsewhere, sold by Novo Nordisk under the Ozempic, Wegovy and Rybelsus names, and as a generic by several companies in the Indian and Canadian markets [1]. Biosimilar-style products are the subject of registered comparison trials, for example a phase 3 study comparing a semaglutide injection with Wegovy for weight loss [29].

Semaglutide appears across fitness and appearance forums. T Nation members mention it in training logs alongside testosterone replacement and other peptides, and a clinic-affiliated poster tagged semaglutide among hormone-therapy services [26][27][28]. On looksmax.org, threads on appetite control and on a "leanmaxxing" face fat protocol discuss drugs as part of lean-face strategies [23][24]. Anthropological work cited on Wikipedia describes patients and clinicians adjusting dose, timing and access in practice, complicating the public view of the drug as an easy option [1].

Semaglutide has been studied in many randomized trials. For weight management, STEP 1 (obesity without diabetes), STEP 2 (with type 2 diabetes), STEP 4 (maintenance), STEP 5 (two years) and STEP 8 (versus liraglutide) are the principal publications [14][9][10][13][12]. The SELECT trial tested semaglutide in people with obesity and established cardiovascular disease but no diabetes [11], and SUSTAIN-6 tested it in type 2 diabetes with cardiovascular risk [15]. Other randomized trials have examined heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity [19], chronic kidney disease in type 2 diabetes [20] and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis [18]. A phase 3b trial compared tirzepatide with semaglutide [3], and a network meta-analysis compared them in type 2 diabetes [21]. No published trial has tested semaglutide specifically for facial appearance.

timeline.event: A phase 1 trial of dosing conditions for the long-acting GLP-1 analogue begins at Novo Nordisk (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01572753).
SUSTAIN-6 reports cardiovascular outcomes of semaglutide in type 2 diabetes [15].
First US approval (Ozempic) for type 2 diabetes [1].
STEP 1 reports weight outcomes of semaglutide 2.4 mg in adults with obesity [14].
SELECT reports cardiovascular outcomes in obesity without diabetes [11].
Head-to-head trial of tirzepatide versus semaglutide in obesity is published [3].

lore.intro: Semaglutide is the most widely discussed GLP-1 drug in fitness and appearance circles, framed mainly as a way to reduce appetite and lean the body and face, with ongoing debate over facial volume loss and muscle retention [22][23][25].

claims.claim: Semaglutide leans the face as total body fat falls.
claims.believers: Men posting on r/MenOnSema describe visible facial fat loss as their weight drops, and looksmax.org threads treat leanness as a route to sharper facial definition [22][24].
claims.experts: The drug is not known to act on facial fat selectively; trials measured total body weight and body composition, not facial change [6][17].

claims.claim: Rapid loss can produce "Ozempic face", a hollowed or aged look.
claims.believers: Users and commentators describe gauntness and sagging after fast loss, and some treat it as a cost to manage [22].
claims.experts: A 2024 dermatology review discusses the phenomenon as a social-media term and examines whether it differs from ordinary weight-loss-related facial change [17].

claims.claim: Most weight lost on GLP-1 drugs is muscle unless you resistance-train.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster states that most of the loss is muscle when no resistance training is done [25].
claims.experts: A 2025 network meta-analysis found lean mass made up about a quarter of total weight lost and that relative lean mass was unchanged for GLP-1 receptor agonists as a group; resistance training was not tested in that analysis [6].

claims.claim: Semaglutide combines well with testosterone therapy and other peptides for physique goals.
claims.believers: Forum logs list semaglutide beside testosterone, BPC-157 and supplements, and a clinic poster bundles it with hormone therapy [26][27].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested such combinations for physique or appearance; label warnings describe the drug alone [16].

claims.claim: Gray-market or compounded semaglutide is an equivalent substitute for the branded drug.
claims.believers: Posters describe sourcing peptide vials and tracking their own results [26].
claims.experts: The trials and the label concern the manufacturer's prescription products; no published trial has tested compounded or research-labelled supplies [16][14].

claims.claim: Weight stays off after stopping once the habit is built.
claims.believers: Some users present short courses as a reset for appetite and eating habits [23].
claims.experts: A 2025 meta-analysis and a Wikipedia-cited review report substantial regain after discontinuation, averaging about two-thirds within a year [7][1].
